mainTopic: Presuming a far-away or endangered person is alive: future versus past death, a חטאת sent from overseas, and people in danger or condemned to death.
overview: The amud opens with רבא answering a contradiction. We do not worry that a far-away husband already died, but we may worry that he will die. After a challenge from the wineskin case and a failed defense, רבא settles on this: 'perhaps he died' is not a worry for anyone, while 'perhaps he will die' is a מחלוקת תנאים. The גמרא then explains how a חטאת sent from overseas can be offered without סמיכה: either it is a woman's offering (רב יוסף) or a bird חטאת (רב פפא). It also shows why the משנה had to teach the presumption of life for גט, תרומה, and חטאת העוף alike. A new משנה follows. People in a besieged town, on a storm-tossed ship, or going to trial are presumed alive. People in a conquered town, on a lost ship, or going to execution get the stringencies of both the living and the dead. רב יוסף limits the execution case to a Jewish court, and the גמרא tests this against bribery, the משנה in מכות, and a ברייתא about death reports. A second version of רב יוסף's statement begins at the end and continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Past death is not a worry, future death is
steps.stepSummary: רבא settles the contradiction: we do not suspect that the husband already died, but we do suspect that he may die soon.
steps.simpleTranslation: We are not concerned that perhaps he already died; we are concerned that perhaps he will die.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the contradiction between the משנה (the wife keeps eating תרומה) and the ברייתא (a גט 'one hour before death' stops her from eating right away). He does it by splitting two kinds of worry.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, the only question is whether the husband has already died, and we do not worry about that. In the ברייתא, the גט depends on a death that could come at any moment in the future, and we do worry about that. So the two sources deal with two different worries and do not contradict.

keyTerms.meaning: perhaps he will die (in the future)
we are concerned / we take this worry into account

phrases.english: That perhaps he died, we are not concerned;
phrases.notes: This is the משנה's case, where the wife keeps eating תרומה.

phrases.english: that perhaps he will die, we are concerned.
phrases.notes: This is the ברייתא's case of a גט that takes effect one hour before his death.

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁמָּא מֵת לָא חָיְישִׁינַן, שֶׁמָּא יָמוּת חָיְישִׁינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction between the משנה and the ברייתא raised just before this section.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction between cases (past doubt versus future doubt)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה and the ברייתא seem to disagree about whether we presume the husband is alive.
steps.terutzMaskana: They deal with different worries: a past death is not suspected, a future death is.

steps.title: The wineskin case is also a future worry, yet תנאים argue
steps.stepSummary: רב אדא בר מתנה points out that the wineskin case is a worry about the future, and there רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה disagree.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אדא בר מתנה said to רבא: But the wineskin case is like 'perhaps he will die,' and they disagree there!
steps.whatsHappening: רב אדא בר מתנה challenges רבא. He shows a case with a future worry where the תנאים argue, so it cannot be a simple rule that we always worry about the future.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the wineskin case, the worry is that the wineskin might burst before the person separates תרומה and מעשר. That is a future worry, just like 'perhaps he will die.' Since the תנאים argue about it, רבא's flat rule 'we worry about the future' seems to go against one side.

keyTerms.meaning: a wineskin (a leather bag for wine)

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַדָּא בַּר מַתְנָה לְרָבָא:
phrases.english: Rav Adda bar Mattana said to Rava:
But the wineskin is like 'perhaps he will die,'
phrases.notes: The worry there is that the wineskin might burst later, before תרומה is separated. It is a future worry.

phrases.english: and they disagree!
phrases.notes: He means רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה, who argue about the wineskin case.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַדָּא בַּר מַתְנָה לְרָבָא: וְהָא נוֹד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבא's distinction from step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's rule that we always worry about a future death (step 1).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The wineskin case is also a future worry, and תנאים argue about it. So 'we worry about the future' is not agreed by everyone.

steps.title: A wineskin is different because a guard can watch it
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה מדסקרתא defends רבא: a wineskin can be handed to a guard, so the worry that it will burst is weaker.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה of Diskarta said: A wineskin is different, because it is possible to hand it over to a guard.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה מדסקרתא answers the challenge to רבא. He says the wineskin is a special case and does not prove anything about worrying over a future death.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The side that does not worry in the wineskin case may only hold that way because a guard can protect the wineskin from bursting. Nobody can guard a person from dying. So the wineskin argument does not touch רבא's rule about death.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda of Diskarta said:
A wineskin is different,
since it is possible that he hands it over to a guard.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה מִדִּסְקַרְתָּא: שָׁאנֵי נוֹד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends רבא against רב אדא בר מתנה's challenge.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The wineskin seems exactly like a future death.
steps.terutzMaskana: A wineskin can be guarded and a person's death cannot, so the cases are not the same.

steps.title: The guard himself needs someone to watch him
steps.stepSummary: רב משרשיא rejects the defense: a guard might be careless, so the wineskin could still burst.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב משרשיא challenged it: Your guarantor needs a guarantor!
steps.whatsHappening: רב משרשיא attacks רב יהודה מדסקרתא's answer. He says handing the wineskin to a guard does not solve anything.
steps.deeperAnalysis: How do we know the guard will do his job? He could be careless, and the wineskin could still burst. So the guard does not remove the future worry, and the wineskin case is again just like a future death.

keyTerms.meaning: a guarantor (someone who backs up another)

phrases.english: Rav Mesharshiya challenged it:
Your guarantor needs a guarantor!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַב מְשַׁרְשְׁיָא: עָרְבָיךְ עָרְבָא צְרִיךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Knocks down the defense given in step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יהודה מדסקרתא's claim that a guard makes the wineskin different.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A guard is not reliable enough to remove the worry, so the wineskin stays a true future worry, and רב אדא's challenge comes back.

steps.title: רבא's new answer: a future death is a מחלוקת תנאים
steps.stepSummary: רבא changes his answer. Everyone agrees we do not worry that he already died, but whether we worry that he will die is argued by תנאים.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: Perhaps he died, we are not concerned; perhaps he will die, it is a dispute of תנאים.
steps.whatsHappening: Since the defense failed, רבא gives a new answer. He no longer claims that everyone worries about the future.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first part stays the same: everyone agrees we do not worry that the husband already died, which explains the משנה. The second part changes: whether we worry about a future death is a מחלוקת תנאים, as in the wineskin case. So the ברייתא simply follows the תנא who does worry.

keyTerms.meaning: rather (drops the earlier answer and gives a new one)
it is a dispute among the תנאים

steps.whatToRemember: Final answer: nobody worries that a far-away person already died. Whether we worry that he will die in the future is a מחלוקת תנאים.

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:
That perhaps he died, we are not concerned;
that perhaps he will die, it is a dispute of tannaim.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the failed answer from step 1 after the defense in step 3 was rejected in step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Attributing the sources to a dispute of תנאים
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Everyone worries about a future death.
steps.terutzMaskana: Everyone agrees we do not suspect a past death; a future death is a מחלוקת תנאים, and the ברייתא follows the side that worries.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The משנה is agreed by all; the ברייתא follows one side of a מחלוקת תנאים.

steps.title: How can the חטאת be offered without סמיכה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה about a חטאת sent from overseas and asks: the owner must lean his hands on his offering, and he is not here!
steps.simpleTranslation: 'One who sends his sin-offering from overseas, etc.': But we need leaning of the hands!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new line in the משנה: a person overseas sends his חטאת, and it is offered. It immediately challenges this, because the owner normally has to do סמיכה himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner is far away, so he cannot lean his hands on the animal. If סמיכה is required, how can the משנה say his חטאת is brought? The גמרא must find a kind of offering that does not need סמיכה.

keyTerms.meaning: the owner leaning his hands on the animal's head before it is offered

phrases.english: 'One who sends his sin-offering from overseas, etc.':
But we need leaning of the hands!

steps.triggerLanguage: הַשּׁוֹלֵחַ חַטָּאתוֹ מִמְּדִינַת הַיָּם וְכוּ׳: וְהָא בָּעֵינָא סְמִיכָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: the next case in the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that a חטאת sent from overseas is offered.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An offering needs סמיכה by its owner, and an owner who is overseas cannot do it.

steps.title: רב יוסף: the משנה means a woman's offering
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף answers that the משנה is talking about an offering brought by a woman, and women do not do סמיכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: It is talking about the offering of women.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף answers the question about סמיכה. He says the משנה is talking about a woman who sent her offering.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Women are not required to do סמיכה on their offerings. So the owner being far away is not a problem, and the offering can be brought.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
With the offering of women.
phrases.notes: Women don't do סמיכה, so the owner's absence doesn't matter.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about סמיכה from step 6.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה seems to describe any חטאת, which would need סמיכה.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה is about a woman's offering, which has no סמיכה.

steps.title: רב פפא: the משנה means a bird חטאת
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא gives a different answer: the משנה is talking about a bird sin-offering, which has no סמיכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: It is talking about a bird sin-offering.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא offers another way to answer the same question about סמיכה. He says the משנה is talking about a bird חטאת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: סמיכה is not done on bird offerings at all. So even a man's offering works, as long as it is a bird. This lets the משנה apply to men too, not only women.

keyTerms.meaning: a sin-offering that is a bird

steps.whatToRemember: The חטאת sent from overseas must be a kind with no סמיכה. רב יוסף says a woman's offering, and רב פפא says a bird חטאת.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
With a bird sin-offering.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second answer to the same question, different from רב יוסף's answer in step 7.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה seems to describe an animal חטאת, which needs סמיכה.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה is about a bird חטאת, which has no סמיכה.

steps.title: Why the case of a bill of divorce alone was not enough
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that the משנה needed to teach both גט and תרומה. A rule about גט could not have taught us the rule about תרומה.
steps.simpleTranslation: All the cases are needed. If the משנה had only taught גט, I would say we rely on him being alive only because there is no other way. But with תרומה, where there is another way, I would say we do not rely on it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the משנה repeated the same rule ('he is presumed alive') in several cases. It starts by showing that the case of גט alone would not have been enough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a גט, if we worried that the husband died, no one could ever send a גט through a messenger. So we have no choice but to presume he is alive. With תרומה, the wife can simply eat regular food, so we might have thought we should be careful and worry that he died.

keyTerms.meaning: It is necessary, meaning each case teaches something the others could not.
Possible, meaning there is another way to manage
The holy portion of produce given to a כהן, which his household may eat

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new argument against the משנה. It is a standard explanation of why the משנה listed several cases that share the same rule.

phrases.english: And it is necessary; for if it had taught us only a bill of divorce,
that would be because it is not possible otherwise,
phrases.notes: He means: if we worried the husband had died, there would be no way to ever send a גט through a messenger.

phrases.english: but with תרומה, where it is possible to manage otherwise,
I would say no, we do not rely on the presumption.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After resolving the סמיכה question about the חטאת, the גמרא steps back to explain why the משנה listed all its cases.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A rule about גט cannot teach the rule about תרומה, because with a גט there is no alternative to relying on the presumption.

steps.title: Why the case of תרומה was also not enough, so all cases are needed
steps.stepSummary: Even with both גט and תרומה, we would not know the rule for חטאת העוף. The concern there is bringing something unholy into the עזרה. So all the cases are needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the משנה had taught only תרומה, I would say we are lenient because sometimes she has no other choice. But with a bird sin-offering, I would say that because of a doubt, we should not bring non-holy things into the Temple courtyard. So all the cases are needed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes explaining why each case was needed. It shows that the חטאת העוף case teaches something new, and concludes that all of them are necessary.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With תרומה, there are times the wife has nothing else to eat, so we might be lenient. With a bird sin-offering, if the owner already died, the bird may not be offered. Bringing it in would be like bringing an unholy animal into the עזרה, so we might have been strict. The משנה teaches that even here we presume he is alive.

keyTerms.meaning: A bird brought as a sin-offering
The courtyard of the בית המקדש

steps.whatToRemember: The rule 'we presume he is still alive' had to be taught for גט, תרומה, and חטאת העוף. Each case has its own reason we might have been stricter or more lenient.

phrases.english: And if it had taught us only תרומה,
that would be because sometimes it is not possible otherwise;
phrases.notes: For example, she might not have enough regular food to eat.

phrases.english: but with a bird sin-offering,
because of a doubt, one should not bring non-holy items into the Temple courtyard,
phrases.notes: If the owner already died, the bird can't be offered, so it would be like bringing an unholy animal into the courtyard.

phrases.english: therefore it is necessary to teach all of them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the explanation of why all the cases are needed, which began in the previous step.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: All three cases are necessary. Each one carries its own reason we might have ruled differently, and the משנה teaches that the presumption of life applies in all of them.

steps.title: New משנה: three dangerous situations where people are still presumed alive
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר בן פרטא taught three cases, and the חכמים accepted them. In these cases the person is in danger but is still presumed alive: a besieged town, a storm-tossed ship, and someone going to trial.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר בן פרטא said three things before the חכמים, and they agreed with him. A town surrounded by an enemy army, a ship being tossed at sea, and a person going out to be judged are all presumed to be alive.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It lists three situations of danger where we still treat the people involved as alive.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In each of these cases the danger is real, but most people come out of it alive. A siege may not end in conquest, a ship in a storm usually survives, and a trial may end in acquittal. So the normal presumption that the person is alive stays in place.

keyTerms.meaning: An enemy army camp surrounding a town
A ship being tossed about in a storm
One going out to be judged in a capital case
The presumption that they are alive

phrases.english: MISHNA: Three things

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן פַּרְטָא לִפְנֵי חֲכָמִים,
phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar ben Perata said before the Sages,
and they upheld his words:
concerning a town that an enemy camp surrounded,
and concerning a ship being tossed about at sea,
and concerning one who goes out to be judged,
that they are presumed to be alive.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁלֹשָׁה דְּבָרִים אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן פַּרְטָא לִפְנֵי חֲכָמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new משנה that continues the theme of presuming a person is alive, now applied to situations of danger.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In a besieged town, on a storm-tossed ship, or when going to trial, people keep their presumption of being alive.

steps.title: Three more severe situations where we are strict both as if alive and as if dead
steps.stepSummary: In a conquered town, a ship lost at sea, or when someone goes out to be executed, we apply the stringencies of both the living and the dead. So neither a בת ישראל married to a כהן nor a בת כהן married to a ישראל may eat תרומה.
steps.simpleTranslation: But for a town that was conquered, a ship that was lost at sea, or a person going out to be executed, we apply the strict rules of both the living and the dead. A בת ישראל married to a כהן, and a בת כהן married to a ישראל, may not eat תרומה.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה contrasts the first three cases with three much more dangerous ones. Here the person loses the presumption of being alive, so we must be strict in both directions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In these cases death is very likely, so we cannot rely on the presumption of life. But we also cannot be sure the person died. So we take the strict side of each possibility. A בת ישראל may eat תרומה only if her כהן husband is alive, and a בת כהן may go back to eating it only if her ישראל husband died. Since either could be true, neither woman eats.

keyTerms.meaning: The stringencies of the living and the stringencies of the dead
A non-כהן woman, who eats תרומה only through her כהן husband
A כהן's daughter, who eats תרומה again only once her ישראל husband dies (if they had no children)

steps.confusionAlert: Both women are forbidden, but for opposite reasons. The בת ישראל is forbidden because maybe her husband died. The בת כהן is forbidden because maybe her husband is still alive.
steps.whatToRemember: Normal danger keeps the presumption of life. Extreme danger removes it, so we are strict both ways.

phrases.english: But a town that an enemy camp conquered,
and a ship that was lost at sea,
and one who goes out to be executed,

phrases.aramaic: נוֹתְנִין עֲלֵיהֶן חוּמְרֵי חַיִּים וְחוּמְרֵי מֵתִים –
phrases.english: we apply to them the stringencies of the living and the stringencies of the dead:
an Israelite woman married to a priest,
and a priest's daughter married to an Israelite,
may not eat תרומה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה by contrasting the first three cases with three more severe situations.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In a conquered town, a lost ship, or when going to execution, we are strict as if the person is alive and as if dead, so neither kind of wife may eat תרומה.

steps.title: רב יוסף limits the משנה to a Jewish court
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף says the משנה's rule only applies to a Jewish court. A non-Jewish court that has sentenced someone to death will surely kill him.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: רב יוסף says: The משנה taught this only about a Jewish court. But in a court of the nations of the world, once he is sentenced to death, they surely kill him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins discussing the משנה's case of someone going out to be executed. רב יוסף limits that case to a Jewish court.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה treats the condemned man as possibly still alive. רב יוסף explains why: a Jewish court can still bring him back if it finds a reason to free him. A non-Jewish court does not do that, so its condemned man is treated as dead.

keyTerms.meaning: They only taught this about... (a phrase that limits a rule)

steps.whyThisMatters: This line sets up the whole סוגיא. Everything that follows tests whether רב יוסף's split between a Jewish court and a non-Jewish court holds up.

phrases.english: GEMARA: Rav Yosef says:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא בְּבֵית דִּין שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל;
phrases.english: They taught this only about a Jewish court;
phrases.notes: "This" means the משנה's case of someone going out to be executed, where we treat him as both alive and dead.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל בְּבֵית דִּין שֶׁל אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם,
phrases.english: but in a court of the nations of the world,
once his sentence is finalized for death,
they surely kill him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the משנה's case from Step 12 of someone going out to be executed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The משנה's rule applies only to a Jewish court. A man sentenced to death by a non-Jewish court is treated as dead.

steps.title: אביי: non-Jewish courts take bribes
steps.stepSummary: אביי argues that a non-Jewish court might also not carry out the sentence, because it can be bribed.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: In a non-Jewish court too, he might not be killed, since they accept bribes!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי challenges רב יוסף's claim that a non-Jewish court will certainly kill the condemned man.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף's split depends on the non-Jewish sentence being final. אביי says it is not final, because a bribe could free the man. If so, the non-Jewish case should match the Jewish one.

phrases.english: Abaye said to him:

phrases.aramaic: בֵּית דִּין שֶׁל אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם נָמֵי,
phrases.english: A court of the nations of the world as well,
phrases.notes: He means: they too might not end up killing him.

phrases.english: since they accept bribes!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reasoning of Step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יוסף's claim that a non-Jewish court surely kills.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Bribery could save the man, so the non-Jewish sentence is not final either.

steps.title: Bribes only work before the verdict is sealed
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף answers that non-Jewish courts take bribes only before the verdict is signed and sealed, not after.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: When they take bribes, it is before the verdict is sealed. After the verdict has been sealed, they do not take bribes.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף defends his position against אביי's challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף agrees that bribes happen. He says they stop once the written verdict is sealed. Our case is a man already sentenced and going out to die, so no bribe can save him, and he is treated as dead.

phrases.english: He said to him:
When they take bribes,
it is before the verdict is sealed;
phrases.notes: פורסי שנמג is a borrowed word for the official written verdict.

phrases.english: after the verdict has been sealed,
they do not take bribes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's challenge from Step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the timing: bribes are taken only before the verdict is sealed.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Bribes could free a man at any stage.
steps.terutzMaskana: After the verdict is sealed, there are no bribes, so the sentence is final.

steps.title: Challenge from מכות: a convicted man is simply executed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a משנה: if witnesses testify that a man was sentenced to death in a certain court, he is executed. This suggests that even a Jewish court's sentence is final.
steps.simpleTranslation: They raised an objection: Any place where two witnesses stand up and say, 'We testify that so-and-so was sentenced in so-and-so's court, and so-and-so and so-and-so were his witnesses,' this man should be killed!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a משנה from מכות to challenge רב יוסף's view that a Jewish court's condemned man may still be saved.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף said a Jewish court might free a condemned man even at the last moment. The משנה in מכות, however, has the man executed based only on the old verdict. It shows no worry that the court might have found a reason to free him, so a Jewish verdict looks final.

keyTerms.meaning: They raised an objection (usually from a משנה or ברייתא)

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
Any place where two witnesses stand up and say:
phrases.notes: This is a משנה in מכות ז. about someone who ran away after being sentenced.

phrases.english: "We testify about so-and-so

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁנִּגְמַר דִּינוֹ בְּבֵית דִּינוֹ שֶׁל פְּלוֹנִי,
phrases.english: that his sentence was finalized in so-and-so's court,
and so-and-so and so-and-so were his witnesses,"
this man should be killed!

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵיתִיבִי, כׇּל מָקוֹם שֶׁיַּעַמְדוּ שְׁנַיִם וְיֹאמְרוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב יוסף's statement from Step 13 with an outside source.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יוסף's idea that a Jewish court's condemned man is still possibly alive.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה carries out a Jewish court's old verdict without worrying that the court might reverse it, so the verdict is final.

steps.title: A runaway is different
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the man in the משנה in מכות had run away, and a runaway is a special case.
steps.simpleTranslation: Perhaps one who runs away is different.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes aside the challenge from מכות by saying the case there is unusual.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה in מכות is about a man who ran away after his sentence. Once he ran away, the court no longer looks for reasons to free him. That does not tell us anything about an ordinary condemned man, so רב יוסף's view still stands.

phrases.english: Perhaps one who runs away is different.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Making a distinction: the source is about a special case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה in מכות proves every Jewish verdict is final.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only a runaway's verdict is treated as final. An ordinary condemned man can still be saved.

steps.title: Death reports from a Jewish court versus non-Jewish officials
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a source. If a Jewish court says a man died or was killed, his wife may remarry. If non-Jewish court officials say so, she may not. This seems to go against רב יוסף.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: If someone heard a Jewish court saying 'So-and-so died' or 'So-and-so was killed,' they let his wife remarry. If he heard non-Jewish court officials say 'So-and-so died' or 'So-and-so was killed,' they do not let his wife remarry.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another source that looks like it points the other way from רב יוסף. The גמרא is setting up a challenge that it will spell out in the next lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key half is the Jewish court: when its report says 'he died' or 'he was killed,' the wife may remarry. If that report could mean he was only being led out to execution, a Jewish court's sentence would be treated as surely carried out, which goes against רב יוסף. The next steps (19–20) work out what 'died' and 'was killed' mean.

keyTerms.meaning: Non-Jewish court officials who keep the court's records

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two halves. The Jewish court's report allows the wife to remarry, and the non-Jewish officials' report does not.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
If one heard from a Jewish court
that they were saying, "So-and-so died";
or "So-and-so was killed",
they let his wife remarry.
If he heard it from non-Jewish court officials,
"So-and-so died" or "So-and-so was killed",
they do not let his wife remarry.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: שְׁמַע מִבֵּית דִּין שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the challenge from מכות was pushed aside in Step 17, the גמרא brings a new source to test רב יוסף.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יוסף's split between a Jewish court and a non-Jewish court.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If 'died' in the Jewish-court case means only being led out to execution, the wife may still remarry. Then a Jewish court's condemned man is treated as dead, against רב יוסף. The גמרא spells this out in steps 19–20.

steps.title: What do 'died' and 'was killed' mean in the ברייתא?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what 'died' and 'was killed' mean in the ברייתא. It tests the plain meaning, that he really died, and finds a problem with it: a non-Jew speaking casually is normally believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'died' mean, and what does 'was killed' mean? Suppose they mean he really died and was really killed. Then the same must be true in the case of the non-Jews. So why can't his wife remarry? We hold that anyone who speaks casually, without meaning to testify, is believed!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what the words 'died' and 'was killed' mean in the ברייתא. It shows that the simple meaning, that he really died, leads to a problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If 'died' means really died, then the non-Jewish officials are reporting an actual death. We usually believe a non-Jew who mentions a death casually (מסיח לפי תומו), so the wife should be allowed to remarry. Since the ברייתא says she may not, the simple meaning seems wrong. This sets up the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: If you will say; it opens a suggestion that is about to be rejected
Speaking casually, without meaning to testify

phrases.english: What is 'died,' and what is 'was killed'?
phrases.notes: These are the two words from the ברייתא quoted in step 18.

phrases.english: If you say 'died' means he actually died,
and 'was killed' means he was actually killed;
then the same applies to the case with the non-Jews,
so why may they not let his wife remarry?
But we hold
that any non-Jew who speaks casually
is believed!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts working out the ברייתא from step 18 so the challenge against רב יוסף can be made clear.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether 'died' and 'was killed' mean an actual death or only being led out to execution.

steps.title: So 'died' must mean going out to die, which goes against רב יוסף
steps.stepSummary: Since the plain meaning did not work, the גמרא suggests that 'died' means 'going out to be executed.' Then the ברייתא says a Jewish court's sentence is assumed to be carried out, which is against רב יוסף.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, doesn't 'died' mean he was going out to die, and 'was killed' mean he was going out to be executed? And the ברייתא teaches that in a Jewish court they let his wife remarry!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reads 'died' as 'being led out to execution.' With that reading, the ברייתא becomes a direct challenge to רב יוסף.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If 'died' means only that he was led out, the ברייתא still lets the wife remarry when it was a Jewish court. That means a Jewish court's sentence is treated as final. But רב יוסף said a Jewish court might still find a reason to spare him, so we cannot be sure he was executed.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, is it not that; it pushes toward the only other reading

phrases.english: Rather, isn't it that 'died' means going out to die,
and 'was killed' means going out to be executed?
And it teaches: in a Jewish court
they let his wife remarry!
phrases.notes: This would mean a Jewish court's sentence is treated as surely carried out, the opposite of what רב יוסף said.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the rejection of the plain meaning in step 19 to force a reading that challenges רב יוסף.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יוסף's view that a Jewish court's death sentence is not assumed to be carried out
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If 'died' means only being led out, and the ברייתא still lets the wife remarry in a Jewish court, then a Jewish court's sentence is treated as final.

steps.title: Really died, but non-Jews back up their own verdict
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא keeps the plain meaning: he really died. Casual speech by a non-Jew is believed only in matters that do not involve them. When it involves their own court, they tend to support their own false verdict.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really, 'died' means he actually died, and 'was killed' means he was actually killed. You asked why the non-Jews are not believed, since anyone speaking casually is believed. That rule applies only to a matter they are not involved in. But in a matter they are involved in, they tend to back up their own lie.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by keeping the meaning 'really died.' It explains why non-Jewish officials are still not believed in this case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Casual speech is believed only when the speaker has nothing at stake. Here the non-Jewish officials are talking about their own court's verdict. They may claim the man was executed just to make their ruling look carried out, even if it wasn't. So the ברייתא never spoke about a man being led out, and there is no challenge to רב יוסף.

keyTerms.meaning: Really, in truth; it keeps the original reading
They are involved in, connected to

steps.whatToRemember: Casual speech (מסיח לפי תומו) is believed only when the speaker has nothing at stake. Non-Jewish officials reporting their own court's execution are not believed, so the ברייתא does not challenge רב יוסף.

phrases.english: Really, he actually died and was actually killed,

phrases.aramaic: וּדְקָאָמְרַתְּ: דִּכְווֹתֵיהּ גַּבֵּי גּוֹיִם אַמַּאי לָא,
phrases.english: and as for what you said: in the same case with the non-Jews, why not,
since we hold

phrases.aramaic: דְּכֹל מֵסִיחַ לְפִי תּוּמּוֹ הֵימוֹנֵי מְהֵימְנִי;
phrases.english: that anyone who speaks casually is believed;

phrases.aramaic: הָנֵי מִילֵּי בְּמִילְּתָא דְּלָא שָׁיְיכִי בָּהּ,
phrases.english: that applies to a matter they are not involved in,
but in a matter they are involved in,
they tend to back up their own lie.
phrases.notes: He means they may say the man was executed just to make their verdict look carried out.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of steps 19–20 by keeping the plain reading and limiting the rule of מסיח לפי תומו.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the rule about casual speech to cases where the speaker has nothing at stake
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Casual speech by a non-Jew is always believed, so 'died' could not mean an actual death.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Died' means an actual death. Non-Jewish officials are not believed because they are backing up their own court's verdict.

steps.title: A second version of רב יוסף's statement begins
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings another version of what רב יוסף said. In this version, the rule applies only to a non-Jewish court. The statement continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say that רב יוסף said: They taught this only about a court of the non-Jewish nations,
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is starting a different version (איכא דאמרי) of רב יוסף's statement. This is setup, and the full statement comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version, רב יוסף limited the rule to a Jewish court. Here he says the rule was taught only about a non-Jewish court. The reason and the rest of the statement come in the next lines.

keyTerms.meaning: Some say; it introduces a second version

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new opinion that argues with step 21. It is a different report of what רב יוסף himself said.

phrases.english: Some say
רב יוסף said:
They taught this only
about a court of the non-Jewish nations,
phrases.notes: This is the reverse of the first version, where רב יוסף limited the rule to a Jewish court.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first version's challenges are settled, the גמרא gives a different report of רב יוסף's statement.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In this version, רב יוסף says the rule was taught only about a non-Jewish court. The rest continues on the next amud.
